result: {"verdict":"findings","summary":"Independent MR-3 readiness review of the installed lifecycle/recovery surface (delegated cgroup ownership, restart-with-descendants, journal cleanup independence, transport/keepalive, upgrade). Verdict: findings — I would not call this z2 snapshot ready on this lens yet. The core containment/journal doctrine is implemented with unusual discipline (fd-pinned cgroup identity, recursive `populated` emptiness rather than root-exit, `poisoned` commit fencing, seal-before-release ordering, `check()` external-tamper detection, transport failure never used as cleanup proof in `daemon/attached.rs`), and both known issues you flagged are real and locatable in the code. The blockers are concentrated at the edges of that core: (a) the systemd delegation contract is over-specified and fails opaquely exactly in the way systemd 259 was observed to break it, with no external restarter behind it; (b) the orphaned-bridge condition that produced the observed EBUSY has no reconciliation anywhere in the reviewed code; (c) `Bridge::spawn` performs none of the interop validation `keepalive()` performs, and the \"connected with alias absent\" observation suggests the published alias may not be the effective channel at all; (d) the journal has no terminal state for uncertain records and never prunes, so a VM restart/logout (your pending scenario) permanently wedges in-flight records while the store grows monotonically toward refusing all new Invocations; (e) the upgrade barrier is SQLite-only, holds a write transaction across `systemctl stop`, and can leave the service stopped. Explicit uncertainty: `src/runner/linux/launch.rs`, the store/driver layer, the daemon startup inventory/recovery path, `read_frame` bounds, per-Invocation memory/pids limits and the entire Windows side were not provided; several findings below are conditional on those and I mark which. I have not assumed omitted code is absent.","findings":["SEVERITY HIGH — Delegation placement is over-specified and fails opaquely; this is the observed EBUSY. Evidence: `delegate()` in scripts/wsl-service.py requires `current.name in (\"manager\",\".control\")` and `parent.name == \"stillyard.service\"` and `executors == parent/\"executors\"`, where `executors` is a literal absolute path baked into the unit at install time by install-wsl-daemon.py (`/sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-{euid}.slice/user@{euid}.service/app.slice/stillyard.service/executors`). It then writes `parent/cgroup.subtree_control` with no precondition check on `parent/cgroup.procs`. Failure trace, matching your observation that systemd 259 spawns the main executor into the service root even with DelegateSubgroup: (1) helper starts in `stillyard.service` itself -> the name guard raises `service cgroup differs from installed delegation` and the unit fails; or (2) if the guard is passed but any process (the helper itself, or a leftover bridge) sits in the delegation root, the `cgroup.subtree_control` write hits the kernel internal-process constraint and surfaces as a bare `OSError: [Errno 16] EBUSY` with no context about which pid blocked it. `Restart=on-failure` + `RestartSec=2` then blindly retries; the observed \"auto-recovered\" is that retry, not a designed recovery. Second-order availability trace: the unit sets no `StartLimitIntervalSec=`/`StartLimitBurst=`, so the defaults (5 starts / 10s) combined with `RestartSec=2` put five failures at ~8-10s — if the blocking process lingers slightly longer than observed, the unit enters permanent `failed`, and with no Windows S4U task and only a detached ordinary wsl.exe keepalive there is nothing to restart it (the keepalive's `systemctl --user start --no-block` only runs when a new WSL session starts). Remedy: derive `executors` at runtime as `parent/\"executors\"` from /proc/self/cgroup and treat the install-time absolute path as evidence only, not as an equality precondition; before writing subtree_control, read `parent/cgroup.procs` and either migrate self into the `manager` subgroup (legal for the delegatee) or fail with the exact blocking pid/comm; set `StartLimitIntervalSec=0`; record the observed systemd version in the install receipt and gate on it.","SEVERITY HIGH — No bridge singleton or startup reconciliation, so an orphaned bridge is structurally possible; this is the other half of the observed EBUSY. Evidence: the unit sets `KillMode=process` (correct, so executor descendants survive a restart), which means systemd does not kill the bridge child on stop/restart. The only teardown is `impl Drop for Bridge` in src/machine/bridge/linux.rs, which requires graceful unwinding, and `Bridge::spawn` takes no lock, records no pid/pidfd anywhere durable, and does not look for a previous bridge. `daemon/attached.rs` drops the `Driver` on error (thus the `Bridge`), but a SIGKILL, an abort, or a systemd stop that reaches the process before unwind leaves the bridge alive. Failure trace: daemon dies non-gracefully -> bridge (and, per WSL interop semantics, whatever Windows-side process it launched, which `child.kill()` does not necessarily reach) remains inside the service cgroup -> systemd restart -> `delegate()` subtree_control write EBUSY (see prior finding) and/or two bridges concurrently attached to the Windows coordinator. Whether the Windows side fences the stale peer is not determinable from the provided files — `SessionIdentity` carries `authority_epoch`, `executor_incarnation` and `connection_epoch`, which suggests fencing exists, but I did not see the coordinator side and cannot confirm it; that confirmation should be an explicit MR-3 test, not an inference. Remedy: give the bridge its own delegated subgroup (e.g. `stillyard.service/bridge`) and `cgroup.kill` it at daemon startup before spawning, or write a durable bridge record (pid + start_ticks + boot_id) and reconcile it with pidfd_open before `Bridge::spawn`; add a test that SIGKILLs the daemon with a live bridge and then restarts the unit.","SEVERITY HIGH — `Bridge::spawn` performs no validation of the interop socket it passes, and the \"connected with alias absent\" observation implies the alias may not be the effective channel. Evidence: `Bridge::spawn` in src/machine/bridge/linux.rs checks only `interop_socket.is_absolute()` and then `.env_clear().env(\"WSL_INTEROP\", interop_socket)`. `keepalive()` in scripts/wsl-service.py, by contrast, does validate: `socket.parent != Path(\"/run/WSL\")`, `stat.S_ISSOCK`, `st_uid != 0`. The alias `root/interop.sock` is a symlink to a per-session socket and is unlinked only in the `finally` of `keepalive()` on SIGTERM/SIGINT — an abnormal keepalive death (SIGKILL, Windows session end, VM teardown) leaves a dangling or stale alias with no boot/session binding, and nothing on the daemon side ever inspects it. Implications, both directions: (1) if the passed variable is load-bearing, a stale alias yields a generic `Unavailable(\"Windows bridge disconnected: ...\")` indistinguishable from a Windows-side outage, and `daemon/attached.rs` retries at 1 Hz indefinitely (see reconnect-storm finding) with a misleading operator-facing error, and with linger keeping the daemon alive there is no self-healing until a new WSL session republishes; (2) the fact that an early connection succeeded with the alias absent is evidence the variable is *not* load-bearing — i.e. the real channel is an inherited session/interop descriptor whose lifetime is not the keepalive's and is neither recorded nor observed anywhere, which invalidates the design claim in the wsl-service.py docstring that the keepalive \"publishes only a transport alias\" as the transport authority. Either way the MR-3 keepalive/alias story is currently unexercised. Also note the missing ownership check is a (narrow, same-uid-bounded) authority gap: a stale or substituted alias could point the launched Windows CLI at a different /run/WSL server with no complaint. Remedy: before spawn, lstat the alias and require symlink -> parent `/run/WSL`, `S_ISSOCK`, uid 0, plus a keepalive-published receipt whose boot_id matches the current `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`, and return a distinct `Unavailable(\"interop alias stale/absent\")`. Required experiments before acceptance: (a) kill the keepalive, remove the alias, and confirm `machine bridge` fails rather than succeeds; (b) point the alias at a deliberately wrong socket and confirm the launch is refused — this distinguishes case (1) from case (2) definitively.","SEVERITY HIGH — The executor journal has no terminal resolution for uncertain records, so a VM restart or logout permanently wedges every in-flight obligation. Evidence: `Journal::cleanup` in src/runner/linux/journal.rs unconditionally calls `Boundary::reopen(identity)?`, and `Boundary::reopen` in src/runner/linux/cgroup.rs rejects any identity whose `boot_id` differs from the current boot. Three distinct entry paths produce a record that can never be sealed by any code in these files: (a) cross-boot — WSL VM shutdown/logout with unsealed records; every subsequent `cleanup` call returns Err forever; (b) interrupted `create` — `create` commits the record, then calls `Boundary::create`, then commits the boundary identity; a crash in that window leaves `boundary: None` and `cleanup` returns `creation interrupted before boundary identity; cleanup unknown` permanently; (c) the seal gap deliberately exercised by `linux_executor_journal_absence_after_seal_gap_retains_uncertainty` — cgroup removed, seal commit failed, `reopen` now fails on a missing path. Fail-closed is the right *default*, and per your doctrine (no Ticket means no OS release; heartbeat is never cleanup proof) the record must not be silently sealed. But there is no attested or operator-visible closure state either, so each of these permanently retains the Lease/Grant debit and permanently occupies the `active` budget counted by `create` (`filter(|r| r.seal.is_none()).count()`, capped by `MAX_ACTIVE = 1024` and by the `(active+1)*16_384` headroom reservation). Given that VM/logout is on your pending list and no coldboot guarantee is claimed, this is the most likely way an installed system degrades in practice. Uncertainty: a boot-change reconciliation or reset/inventory path may exist outside these files (the module comment \"Reset-independent executor obligations\" hints at one); I did not see it, and every mutator in journal.rs (`create`, `ready`, `release_intent`, `cleanup`) only inserts or sets fields, so it cannot live in this file as written. Remedy: add an explicit `uncertain_closed` terminal state that preserves `possibly_released` and the boundary identity, reachable only via cross-boot reconciliation (a boot_id mismatch is itself durable evidence the kernel boundary is gone) or an audited operator attestation, and surface the count in `daemon-status` so it is a visible blocker rather than silent capacity loss.","SEVERITY HIGH — The journal is append-only with a hard ceiling, so an installed coordinator eventually refuses all new Invocations. Evidence: in src/runner/linux/journal.rs, `State.records` is a `BTreeMap<InvocationId, Record>` and no method removes an entry — sealed records are retained forever, each retaining its full `release_intent` ticket (bounded at 8192 bytes by `release_intent`) plus boundary identity and both process identities. `create` enforces `self.state.records.len() >= MAX_RECORDS` (16,384) and the size guard `serde_json::to_vec(&self.state)?.len() + (active+1)*16_384 > MAX_BYTES - 1024*1024` (a ~15 MiB effective state budget against `MAX_BYTES = 16 MiB`). Failure trace: at a realistic 2-8 KiB serialized per sealed record, the state crosses the 15 MiB reservation after roughly a few thousand completed Invocations; from then on every `create` returns `executor history cleanup headroom unavailable` — cleanup still works (correctly prioritized), but no new work can ever be admitted, and there is no pruning, rotation or archive path in the reviewed code to recover. For a single-machine coordinator expected to run continuously across many Attempts this is a certain, not hypothetical, end state. Secondary cost: `check()` re-reads and re-hashes the entire state on every `records()`/`commit()`, and `create`/`ready`/`release_intent`/`cleanup` each `self.state.clone()` it, so per-Invocation CPU and I/O grow linearly toward a 16 MiB read + SHA-256 + clone per call. Remedy: prune or roll off sealed records into an append-only archive segment (retaining seal digests so idempotent replay of a sealed Invocation still returns the same `Seal`), or key retention on the durable SQLite Attempt lifetime; add a test that drives several thousand seal cycles and asserts admission still succeeds.","SEVERITY MEDIUM-HIGH — The unit omits `OOMPolicy=`, so memory pressure inside an Invocation can stop the coordinator. Evidence: the unit text in install-wsl-daemon.py sets `Delegate=cpu memory pids`, `DelegateSubgroup=manager`, `KillMode=process`, and `delegate()` sets `executors/memory.max` to 16 GiB and `executors/pids.max` to 4096 — but no `OOMPolicy=` is set. systemd's `DefaultOOMPolicy=` for services is `stop`, and for units with `Delegate=` the policy applies to the whole delegated subtree; `memory.events` `oom_kill` is hierarchical, so a kernel OOM kill inside `executors/invocation-*` is visible as a unit-level OOM event. Failure trace: an Invocation drives `executors` to its 16 GiB limit -> kernel OOM-kills a task in the invocation cgroup -> systemd stops stillyard.service -> `KillMode=process` means only the daemon main process is signalled, so the user Invocation's descendants survive as orphans in `executors/invocation-*` while the daemon dies, and per the journal design no seal is written -> the record becomes an uncertain obligation, compounding the two prior findings. This is precisely a fault class in your pending list (actual faults, idle budget) and would not appear in the passing root-exit/cancel/timeout runs. Verification I could not perform (no tools this session): `systemctl --user show stillyard.service -p OOMPolicy` and `systemctl --user show -p DefaultOOMPolicy` on the installed y2 host. Remedy: set `OOMPolicy=continue` explicitly in the unit and confirm no systemd-oomd managed-pressure setting applies to `app.slice`. Related uncertainty: the two limits set here are *collective* to `executors`; per-Invocation `memory.max`/`pids.max` may well be applied by the launch path in src/runner/linux/launch.rs, which was not provided — if they are not, one Invocation can consume the whole budget and all 4096 pids and starve every peer, which is the same trigger.","SEVERITY MEDIUM-HIGH — The upgrade holds a SQLite write transaction across `systemctl stop`, which can deadlock the daemon's own shutdown writes. Evidence: in scripts/upgrade-wsl-daemon.py, `db.execute(\"BEGIN IMMEDIATE\")` is followed by the lease/containment barrier queries, `save(\"barrier.json\", ...)`, and then `subprocess.run([\"systemctl\", \"--user\", \"stop\", \"stillyard.service\"], check=True, timeout=20)` — all inside the transaction, which is only released in the `finally` after `replacement.json`. Failure trace: SIGTERM reaches the daemon -> any store write on the shutdown path blocks on the updater's write lock (src/daemon/attached.rs shows the pattern, calling `store.attached_offline()` before `releases.disconnect()`; generation close-out is likely similar) -> either the daemon's busy timeout expires and shutdown reports spurious store errors, or stop exceeds the unit's `TimeoutStopSec` (unset, so the 90s default) and the `timeout=20` on `subprocess.run` raises `TimeoutExpired` first -> the `finally` rolls back and closes the db, `staged.unlink()` runs, and the tool exits with the unit in `stopping`/`failed` and the binary unreplaced. The intent (hold admission closed across the swap so a failed barrier leaves the daemon running) is sound; using an exclusive SQL write lock as the fence is what breaks. Remedy: take the barrier, record it, `ROLLBACK` before invoking systemctl, stop, confirm exit via the already-held pidfd, then re-open SQLite and re-verify the barrier with the daemon provably gone (no writer can race at that point); or add a daemon-side admission-close RPC and gate on `daemon-status` reporting the fence, rather than on lock contention.","SEVERITY MEDIUM-HIGH — The upgrade barrier is SQLite-only, contradicting the stated cleanup doctrine. Evidence: the docstring claims the tool \"refuses outstanding Leases or containment\", but the barrier in scripts/upgrade-wsl-daemon.py is exactly two queries — `select count(*) from leases where state='granted'` and `select count(*) from containments where state!='empty'`. It never reads the executor journal `state.json` for records with `seal is None`, and never checks actual emptiness of the delegated `executors` cgroup, although src/runner/linux/journal.rs is explicitly built as the reset-independent authority (\"A missing cgroup is never a seal\") and your doctrine requires actual cgroup emptiness plus a durable journal seal. Failure traces: (a) `Journal::create` commits its record before any boundary exists and the SQLite containment row is written by a separate step — a crash in that window leaves an unsealed journal record while the barrier counts zero, so the upgrade proceeds and the new daemon inherits an obligation the barrier declared absent; (b) after any prior non-graceful daemon death under `KillMode=process`, live descendants in `executors/invocation-*` are invisible to both queries. Harm is bounded today by the same-version restriction (`version != \"stillyard \" + before[\"version\"]` -> error) and by preservation of the Store/journal/backup, so this is a doctrine and evidence gap rather than an immediate corruption path — but it is the barrier the upgrade's entire safety claim rests on. Remedy: add the journal (unsealed record count, by boot_id) and a direct `executors` subtree scan (per-child `cgroup.events` `populated`, recursively) to the barrier, and record all three in barrier.json so the evidence shows independent agreement rather than one source.","SEVERITY MEDIUM — A failed upgrade leaves the coordinator stopped, and several safety checks are `assert`s or unchecked. Evidence: in scripts/upgrade-wsl-daemon.py, `subprocess.run([... \"start\", ...])` sits *after* the try/finally, so any exception raised between the successful `systemctl stop` and the end of the try (a rename failure, a `save()` failure on replacement.json, the `staged.exists()` unlink path, a KeyboardInterrupt) propagates with the service stopped and never restarted; with linger and no S4U task, nothing else brings it back, and the keepalive only issues `systemctl --user start` when a fresh WSL session begins. Additionally: `assert digest(staged) == args.candidate_sha256`, `assert after[\"store_uuid\"] == before[\"store_uuid\"]` and `assert after[\"daemon_generation\"] != before[\"daemon_generation\"]` are elided entirely under `python -O`/`PYTHONOPTIMIZE`, so the post-copy integrity check and the store-identity/generation-change checks are not guaranteed to run; and `start.returncode` is written into service-start.json but never tested, so a start failure is only caught indirectly by the 45s `daemon-status` poll, whose error text (\"replacement did not reconnect\") misattributes the cause. Remedy: wrap stop-through-swap in a try/finally that always attempts `systemctl --user start` (restoring the backup first if the swap did not commit), convert the three asserts to explicit raises, and raise on a nonzero `start.returncode` with the captured stderr. Minor related nit in the same file: it invokes bare `systemctl` (PATH-dependent) with no XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS, unlike wsl-service.py which uses `/usr/bin/systemctl` with an explicit env — run from a session without a user bus, `check=True` raises after the barrier is taken.","SEVERITY MEDIUM — Neither installer can deliver a fix to the delegation helper or the unit onto a running system, which blocks the very fix this snapshot needs. Evidence: scripts/upgrade-wsl-daemon.py replaces only `root/bin/stillyard` (it hashes, stages and renames that one path) and never touches `root/libexec/wsl-service.py` or `~/.config/systemd/user/stillyard.service`; it also never compares the installed helper against the `helper_sha256` recorded by install-wsl-daemon.py, so silent drift or hand-editing of the helper/unit is undetected at runtime. scripts/install-wsl-daemon.py refuses to run at all when either exists (`if installed.exists() or unit.exists(): parser.error(\"initial installation refuses an existing executable or service; use an audited upgrade\")`). Failure trace: the systemd-259 delegation problem and the `--executors` hardcoding both live in the helper and the unit, so the z2 fix has no supported delivery path onto the installed y2 host — the only routes are an unaudited manual edit (invisible to all evidence files) or a destructive teardown of the Store the upgrade tool exists to preserve. Remedy: extend the upgrade tool to stage helper and unit under the same barrier (digest-pinned, `daemon-reload` after, both digests in replacement.json), and have `delegate()` verify its own file digest against a recorded anchor at startup so drift fails closed.","SEVERITY MEDIUM — Initial install never binds the installed bytes to the verified release Job; the digest check is circular. Evidence: scripts/install-wsl-daemon.py validates the Job (`state == \"final\"`, `outcome == \"succeeded\"`, label `wsl-bootstrap-build-release`) and separately checks `digest(args.candidate) != args.candidate_sha256` — but `--candidate-sha256` is operator-supplied and is compared only against the operator-supplied `--candidate`, which proves self-consistency and nothing about provenance. Contrast scripts/upgrade-wsl-daemon.py, which does bind them: it derives `target = Path(build[\"spec\"][\"environment\"][\"set\"][\"CARGO_TARGET_DIR\"])/\"release/stillyard\"` and rejects unless `candidate == target.resolve()` and `build[\"spec\"][\"args\"] == [\"build\",\"--locked\",\"--release\"]`. So the tool whose docstring promises \"a validated first WSL installation\" is the weaker of the two: any file at all can be installed alongside a genuine but unrelated successful gate Job, and the resulting plan.json will look fully validated. Remedy: apply the upgrade tool's CARGO_TARGET_DIR/args binding in the install path as well, and record the resolved target path in plan.json.","SEVERITY MEDIUM — Install is neither atomic nor durable, and a crash mid-install wedges both tools. Evidence: scripts/install-wsl-daemon.py uses `shutil.copyfile(args.candidate, installed)` and `shutil.copyfile(source_helper, helper)` directly to their final names (no staged temp + rename, so a truncated interrupt leaves a partial executable at the live path); it fsyncs file contents via read-only handles (`with path.open(\"rb\") as stream: os.fsync(stream.fileno())` — permitted on Linux but fragile) and never fsyncs any containing directory (`root`, `bin`, `libexec`, `~/.config/systemd/user`), unlike the careful `publish()` in src/runner/linux/journal.rs which does `File::open(directory)?.sync_all()` after every rename/link. Failure trace: a VM shutdown or crash after `save(root/\"config.json\", ...)` but before the binary's directory entry is durable leaves `config.json` present and `bin/stillyard` absent or zero-length; re-running install then hits `initial installation refuses existing Store/configuration history`, while upgrade-wsl-daemon.py cannot help because its first action is `query(\"daemon-status\")` against a binary that does not work — manual cleanup of a partially-installed Store becomes the only exit. Given no coldboot guarantee is claimed, this window is reachable. Remedy: copy to `.next-<uuid>` + fsync + rename + parent-directory fsync for binary, helper, config and unit; write an `install-in-progress` marker that install itself is permitted to reconcile, so a partial install is repairable by the tool that created it.","SEVERITY MEDIUM — Cleanup can be permanently blocked by a child cgroup, and the mitigation is only a comment. Evidence: `Boundary::kill_and_seal` in src/runner/linux/cgroup.rs writes `cgroup.kill`, waits on the (correctly recursive) `populated` flag, then ends with `std::fs::remove_dir(&self.identity.path)`; the comment states \"Invocation user code sees read-only cgroups, so it cannot add child boundaries. Unexpected descendants make rmdir fail closed.\" Nothing in the two Linux runner files provided enforces or tests that claim — the invocation cgroup is created by the daemon under the same uid as the Invocation, and per cgroup-v2 delegation semantics a same-uid process with a writable cgroupfs view can `mkdir` inside its own cgroup. Failure trace if the read-only view is not actually in place: user code creates `executors/invocation-X/sub` -> `cgroup.kill` still kills recursively and `populated` goes to 0, so the wait loop exits -> `remove_dir` fails EBUSY on the non-empty cgroup -> `kill_and_seal` returns Err -> `Journal::cleanup` returns Err with no seal -> per doctrine no Ticket, no release, so the Lease/Grant debit is retained forever, and every retry fails identically because the child directory persists. That is a self-inflicted capacity DoS from inside a single Invocation. Uncertainty: src/runner/linux/launch.rs and the namespace/mount setup were not provided; the guarantee may well be implemented there, in which case this reduces to a missing test. Also note `contains_process` reads only the boundary's own `cgroup.procs` and is therefore non-recursive — sound at its one current call site (`Journal::ready`, before user code runs, root directly attached) but a hazard if it is ever reused for cleanup or attribution; the recursive `populated` is correctly the emptiness proof. Remedy: depth-first rmdir of any surviving descendants before removing the boundary; assert the read-only cgroupfs view at attach time; add a hostile-Invocation test that mkdirs a child cgroup and asserts the seal still completes.","SEVERITY MEDIUM-LOW — Reconnect handling amplifies any transport outage. Evidence: the error arm of the loop in src/daemon/attached.rs ends in a fixed `std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1))` with no exponential backoff, jitter, cap, or escalation after N consecutive failures; each retry calls `Driver::connect` -> `Bridge::spawn`, which re-reads and SHA-256s the *entire* Windows image on every attempt (the `loop { image.read(&mut buffer) }` block, bounded only at 512 MiB) across the DrvFs/9p boundary. Also, `exchange()` sets `self.broken = true` before the frame exchange and clears it only after correlation succeeds, so any single `DeadlineElapsed` (deadline clamped to 30s) discards the whole bridge and forces a full respawn plus rehash — correct fail-closed reasoning about stream position, but expensive. Failure trace: a stale interop alias or a Windows-side outage produces sustained 1 Hz respawn attempts, each hashing the Windows binary over the filesystem bridge, for as long as the outage lasts (indefinitely, since with linger the daemon persists); the `reported`-string dedup in the same loop suppresses repeats only while the detail text is byte-identical, so any varying errno/detail floods journald at the same cadence. Remedy: exponential backoff with cap and jitter; cache the verified image digest keyed on (dev, ino, size, mtime) and re-verify on change rather than on every attempt; distinguish and report stale-alias separately (see the interop-validation finding); add a consecutive-failure threshold that surfaces as a `daemon-status` blocker. Minor, same file: the success path does `store.lock().ok().and_then(...).unwrap_or(1s)`, silently degrading a poisoned store mutex to default polling instead of treating it as terminal.","SEVERITY MEDIUM-LOW — Keepalive leaks its alias on start failure, and its recorded lifetime story no longer matches reality. Evidence in scripts/wsl-service.py `keepalive()`: (1) `subprocess.run([\"/usr/bin/systemctl\", \"--user\", \"start\", \"--no-block\", \"stillyard.service\"], check=True, timeout=15)` executes *before* the `try:` whose `finally` unlinks the alias, so a CalledProcessError/TimeoutExpired there exits with a traceback and leaves `root/interop.sock` behind, pointing at a socket that dies with the session — manufacturing exactly the stale-alias state that `Bridge::spawn` does not validate; (2) `--no-block` plus `check=True` verifies only that systemctl accepted the job, never that the service reached running or that the daemon paired, so the component claiming lifetime authority has no readiness feedback; (3) `os.environ[\"WSL_INTEROP\"]` raises a bare KeyError rather than the module's clear RuntimeError style; (4) the published record (`pid`, `boot_id`, `interop_alias`, `interop_server`) goes only to stdout — under the actual deployment (no S4U task, a detached ordinary per-user wsl.exe) that console is not captured, so the one piece of evidence that would let the daemon validate alias freshness against the current boot_id is discarded; (5) the module docstring still asserts \"The Windows scheduled task runs keepalive in a foreground wsl.exe session\", and install-wsl-daemon.py's docstring says \"Windows keepalive registration follow[s] the saved setup receipt\", yet no evidence file records which mechanism is actually in force — a reviewer reading plan.json/staged.json cannot distinguish a registered S4U task from the degraded detached fallback that exists after the access-denied/UAC-cancelled attempt. Remedy: write the receipt durably to `root/keepalive.json` (atomic replace, including boot_id and pid start_ticks) and have `Bridge::spawn` require a match; move the systemctl start inside the try/finally; raise a clear error when WSL_INTEROP is unset; record the actual keepalive mechanism and its privilege outcome in the install evidence and in `daemon-status`."]}

structured_output.summary: Independent MR-3 readiness review of the installed lifecycle/recovery surface (delegated cgroup ownership, restart-with-descendants, journal cleanup independence, transport/keepalive, upgrade). Verdict: findings — I would not call this z2 snapshot ready on this lens yet. The core containment/journal doctrine is implemented with unusual discipline (fd-pinned cgroup identity, recursive `populated` emptiness rather than root-exit, `poisoned` commit fencing, seal-before-release ordering, `check()` external-tamper detection, transport failure never used as cleanup proof in `daemon/attached.rs`), and both known issues you flagged are real and locatable in the code. The blockers are concentrated at the edges of that core: (a) the systemd delegation contract is over-specified and fails opaquely exactly in the way systemd 259 was observed to break it, with no external restarter behind it; (b) the orphaned-bridge condition that produced the observed EBUSY has no reconciliation anywhere in the reviewed code; (c) `Bridge::spawn` performs none of the interop validation `keepalive()` performs, and the "connected with alias absent" observation suggests the published alias may not be the effective channel at all; (d) the journal has no terminal state for uncertain records and never prunes, so a VM restart/logout (your pending scenario) permanently wedges in-flight records while the store grows monotonically toward refusing all new Invocations; (e) the upgrade barrier is SQLite-only, holds a write transaction across `systemctl stop`, and can leave the service stopped. Explicit uncertainty: `src/runner/linux/launch.rs`, the store/driver layer, the daemon startup inventory/recovery path, `read_frame` bounds, per-Invocation memory/pids limits and the entire Windows side were not provided; several findings below are conditional on those and I mark which. I have not assumed omitted code is absent.
findings: SEVERITY HIGH — Delegation placement is over-specified and fails opaquely; this is the observed EBUSY. Evidence: `delegate()` in scripts/wsl-service.py requires `current.name in ("manager",".control")` and `parent.name == "stillyard.service"` and `executors == parent/"executors"`, where `executors` is a literal absolute path baked into the unit at install time by install-wsl-daemon.py (`/sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-{euid}.slice/user@{euid}.service/app.slice/stillyard.service/executors`). It then writes `parent/cgroup.subtree_control` with no precondition check on `parent/cgroup.procs`. Failure trace, matching your observation that systemd 259 spawns the main executor into the service root even with DelegateSubgroup: (1) helper starts in `stillyard.service` itself -> the name guard raises `service cgroup differs from installed delegation` and the unit fails; or (2) if the guard is passed but any process (the helper itself, or a leftover bridge) sits in the delegation root, the `cgroup.subtree_control` write hits the kernel internal-process constraint and surfaces as a bare `OSError: [Errno 16] EBUSY` with no context about which pid blocked it. `Restart=on-failure` + `RestartSec=2` then blindly retries; the observed "auto-recovered" is that retry, not a designed recovery. Second-order availability trace: the unit sets no `StartLimitIntervalSec=`/`StartLimitBurst=`, so the defaults (5 starts / 10s) combined with `RestartSec=2` put five failures at ~8-10s — if the blocking process lingers slightly longer than observed, the unit enters permanent `failed`, and with no Windows S4U task and only a detached ordinary wsl.exe keepalive there is nothing to restart it (the keepalive's `systemctl --user start --no-block` only runs when a new WSL session starts). Remedy: derive `executors` at runtime as `parent/"executors"` from /proc/self/cgroup and treat the install-time absolute path as evidence only, not as an equality precondition; before writing subtree_control, read `parent/cgroup.procs` and either migrate self into the `manager` subgroup (legal for the delegatee) or fail with the exact blocking pid/comm; set `StartLimitIntervalSec=0`; record the observed systemd version in the install receipt and gate on it.

SEVERITY HIGH — No bridge singleton or startup reconciliation, so an orphaned bridge is structurally possible; this is the other half of the observed EBUSY. Evidence: the unit sets `KillMode=process` (correct, so executor descendants survive a restart), which means systemd does not kill the bridge child on stop/restart. The only teardown is `impl Drop for Bridge` in src/machine/bridge/linux.rs, which requires graceful unwinding, and `Bridge::spawn` takes no lock, records no pid/pidfd anywhere durable, and does not look for a previous bridge. `daemon/attached.rs` drops the `Driver` on error (thus the `Bridge`), but a SIGKILL, an abort, or a systemd stop that reaches the process before unwind leaves the bridge alive. Failure trace: daemon dies non-gracefully -> bridge (and, per WSL interop semantics, whatever Windows-side process it launched, which `child.kill()` does not necessarily reach) remains inside the service cgroup -> systemd restart -> `delegate()` subtree_control write EBUSY (see prior finding) and/or two bridges concurrently attached to the Windows coordinator. Whether the Windows side fences the stale peer is not determinable from the provided files — `SessionIdentity` carries `authority_epoch`, `executor_incarnation` and `connection_epoch`, which suggests fencing exists, but I did not see the coordinator side and cannot confirm it; that confirmation should be an explicit MR-3 test, not an inference. Remedy: give the bridge its own delegated subgroup (e.g. `stillyard.service/bridge`) and `cgroup.kill` it at daemon startup before spawning, or write a durable bridge record (pid + start_ticks + boot_id) and reconcile it with pidfd_open before `Bridge::spawn`; add a test that SIGKILLs the daemon with a live bridge and then restarts the unit.

SEVERITY HIGH — `Bridge::spawn` performs no validation of the interop socket it passes, and the "connected with alias absent" observation implies the alias may not be the effective channel. Evidence: `Bridge::spawn` in src/machine/bridge/linux.rs checks only `interop_socket.is_absolute()` and then `.env_clear().env("WSL_INTEROP", interop_socket)`. `keepalive()` in scripts/wsl-service.py, by contrast, does validate: `socket.parent != Path("/run/WSL")`, `stat.S_ISSOCK`, `st_uid != 0`. The alias `root/interop.sock` is a symlink to a per-session socket and is unlinked only in the `finally` of `keepalive()` on SIGTERM/SIGINT — an abnormal keepalive death (SIGKILL, Windows session end, VM teardown) leaves a dangling or stale alias with no boot/session binding, and nothing on the daemon side ever inspects it. Implications, both directions: (1) if the passed variable is load-bearing, a stale alias yields a generic `Unavailable("Windows bridge disconnected: ...")` indistinguishable from a Windows-side outage, and `daemon/attached.rs` retries at 1 Hz indefinitely (see reconnect-storm finding) with a misleading operator-facing error, and with linger keeping the daemon alive there is no self-healing until a new WSL session republishes; (2) the fact that an early connection succeeded with the alias absent is evidence the variable is *not* load-bearing — i.e. the real channel is an inherited session/interop descriptor whose lifetime is not the keepalive's and is neither recorded nor observed anywhere, which invalidates the design claim in the wsl-service.py docstring that the keepalive "publishes only a transport alias" as the transport authority. Either way the MR-3 keepalive/alias story is currently unexercised. Also note the missing ownership check is a (narrow, same-uid-bounded) authority gap: a stale or substituted alias could point the launched Windows CLI at a different /run/WSL server with no complaint. Remedy: before spawn, lstat the alias and require symlink -> parent `/run/WSL`, `S_ISSOCK`, uid 0, plus a keepalive-published receipt whose boot_id matches the current `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`, and return a distinct `Unavailable("interop alias stale/absent")`. Required experiments before acceptance: (a) kill the keepalive, remove the alias, and confirm `machine bridge` fails rather than succeeds; (b) point the alias at a deliberately wrong socket and confirm the launch is refused — this distinguishes case (1) from case (2) definitively.

SEVERITY HIGH — The executor journal has no terminal resolution for uncertain records, so a VM restart or logout permanently wedges every in-flight obligation. Evidence: `Journal::cleanup` in src/runner/linux/journal.rs unconditionally calls `Boundary::reopen(identity)?`, and `Boundary::reopen` in src/runner/linux/cgroup.rs rejects any identity whose `boot_id` differs from the current boot. Three distinct entry paths produce a record that can never be sealed by any code in these files: (a) cross-boot — WSL VM shutdown/logout with unsealed records; every subsequent `cleanup` call returns Err forever; (b) interrupted `create` — `create` commits the record, then calls `Boundary::create`, then commits the boundary identity; a crash in that window leaves `boundary: None` and `cleanup` returns `creation interrupted before boundary identity; cleanup unknown` permanently; (c) the seal gap deliberately exercised by `linux_executor_journal_absence_after_seal_gap_retains_uncertainty` — cgroup removed, seal commit failed, `reopen` now fails on a missing path. Fail-closed is the right *default*, and per your doctrine (no Ticket means no OS release; heartbeat is never cleanup proof) the record must not be silently sealed. But there is no attested or operator-visible closure state either, so each of these permanently retains the Lease/Grant debit and permanently occupies the `active` budget counted by `create` (`filter(|r| r.seal.is_none()).count()`, capped by `MAX_ACTIVE = 1024` and by the `(active+1)*16_384` headroom reservation). Given that VM/logout is on your pending list and no coldboot guarantee is claimed, this is the most likely way an installed system degrades in practice. Uncertainty: a boot-change reconciliation or reset/inventory path may exist outside these files (the module comment "Reset-independent executor obligations" hints at one); I did not see it, and every mutator in journal.rs (`create`, `ready`, `release_intent`, `cleanup`) only inserts or sets fields, so it cannot live in this file as written. Remedy: add an explicit `uncertain_closed` terminal state that preserves `possibly_released` and the boundary identity, reachable only via cross-boot reconciliation (a boot_id mismatch is itself durable evidence the kernel boundary is gone) or an audited operator attestation, and surface the count in `daemon-status` so it is a visible blocker rather than silent capacity loss.

SEVERITY HIGH — The journal is append-only with a hard ceiling, so an installed coordinator eventually refuses all new Invocations. Evidence: in src/runner/linux/journal.rs, `State.records` is a `BTreeMap<InvocationId, Record>` and no method removes an entry — sealed records are retained forever, each retaining its full `release_intent` ticket (bounded at 8192 bytes by `release_intent`) plus boundary identity and both process identities. `create` enforces `self.state.records.len() >= MAX_RECORDS` (16,384) and the size guard `serde_json::to_vec(&self.state)?.len() + (active+1)*16_384 > MAX_BYTES - 1024*1024` (a ~15 MiB effective state budget against `MAX_BYTES = 16 MiB`). Failure trace: at a realistic 2-8 KiB serialized per sealed record, the state crosses the 15 MiB reservation after roughly a few thousand completed Invocations; from then on every `create` returns `executor history cleanup headroom unavailable` — cleanup still works (correctly prioritized), but no new work can ever be admitted, and there is no pruning, rotation or archive path in the reviewed code to recover. For a single-machine coordinator expected to run continuously across many Attempts this is a certain, not hypothetical, end state. Secondary cost: `check()` re-reads and re-hashes the entire state on every `records()`/`commit()`, and `create`/`ready`/`release_intent`/`cleanup` each `self.state.clone()` it, so per-Invocation CPU and I/O grow linearly toward a 16 MiB read + SHA-256 + clone per call. Remedy: prune or roll off sealed records into an append-only archive segment (retaining seal digests so idempotent replay of a sealed Invocation still returns the same `Seal`), or key retention on the durable SQLite Attempt lifetime; add a test that drives several thousand seal cycles and asserts admission still succeeds.

SEVERITY MEDIUM-HIGH — The unit omits `OOMPolicy=`, so memory pressure inside an Invocation can stop the coordinator. Evidence: the unit text in install-wsl-daemon.py sets `Delegate=cpu memory pids`, `DelegateSubgroup=manager`, `KillMode=process`, and `delegate()` sets `executors/memory.max` to 16 GiB and `executors/pids.max` to 4096 — but no `OOMPolicy=` is set. systemd's `DefaultOOMPolicy=` for services is `stop`, and for units with `Delegate=` the policy applies to the whole delegated subtree; `memory.events` `oom_kill` is hierarchical, so a kernel OOM kill inside `executors/invocation-*` is visible as a unit-level OOM event. Failure trace: an Invocation drives `executors` to its 16 GiB limit -> kernel OOM-kills a task in the invocation cgroup -> systemd stops stillyard.service -> `KillMode=process` means only the daemon main process is signalled, so the user Invocation's descendants survive as orphans in `executors/invocation-*` while the daemon dies, and per the journal design no seal is written -> the record becomes an uncertain obligation, compounding the two prior findings. This is precisely a fault class in your pending list (actual faults, idle budget) and would not appear in the passing root-exit/cancel/timeout runs. Verification I could not perform (no tools this session): `systemctl --user show stillyard.service -p OOMPolicy` and `systemctl --user show -p DefaultOOMPolicy` on the installed y2 host. Remedy: set `OOMPolicy=continue` explicitly in the unit and confirm no systemd-oomd managed-pressure setting applies to `app.slice`. Related uncertainty: the two limits set here are *collective* to `executors`; per-Invocation `memory.max`/`pids.max` may well be applied by the launch path in src/runner/linux/launch.rs, which was not provided — if they are not, one Invocation can consume the whole budget and all 4096 pids and starve every peer, which is the same trigger.

SEVERITY MEDIUM-HIGH — The upgrade holds a SQLite write transaction across `systemctl stop`, which can deadlock the daemon's own shutdown writes. Evidence: in scripts/upgrade-wsl-daemon.py, `db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")` is followed by the lease/containment barrier queries, `save("barrier.json", ...)`, and then `subprocess.run(["systemctl", "--user", "stop", "stillyard.service"], check=True, timeout=20)` — all inside the transaction, which is only released in the `finally` after `replacement.json`. Failure trace: SIGTERM reaches the daemon -> any store write on the shutdown path blocks on the updater's write lock (src/daemon/attached.rs shows the pattern, calling `store.attached_offline()` before `releases.disconnect()`; generation close-out is likely similar) -> either the daemon's busy timeout expires and shutdown reports spurious store errors, or stop exceeds the unit's `TimeoutStopSec` (unset, so the 90s default) and the `timeout=20` on `subprocess.run` raises `TimeoutExpired` first -> the `finally` rolls back and closes the db, `staged.unlink()` runs, and the tool exits with the unit in `stopping`/`failed` and the binary unreplaced. The intent (hold admission closed across the swap so a failed barrier leaves the daemon running) is sound; using an exclusive SQL write lock as the fence is what breaks. Remedy: take the barrier, record it, `ROLLBACK` before invoking systemctl, stop, confirm exit via the already-held pidfd, then re-open SQLite and re-verify the barrier with the daemon provably gone (no writer can race at that point); or add a daemon-side admission-close RPC and gate on `daemon-status` reporting the fence, rather than on lock contention.

SEVERITY MEDIUM-HIGH — The upgrade barrier is SQLite-only, contradicting the stated cleanup doctrine. Evidence: the docstring claims the tool "refuses outstanding Leases or containment", but the barrier in scripts/upgrade-wsl-daemon.py is exactly two queries — `select count(*) from leases where state='granted'` and `select count(*) from containments where state!='empty'`. It never reads the executor journal `state.json` for records with `seal is None`, and never checks actual emptiness of the delegated `executors` cgroup, although src/runner/linux/journal.rs is explicitly built as the reset-independent authority ("A missing cgroup is never a seal") and your doctrine requires actual cgroup emptiness plus a durable journal seal. Failure traces: (a) `Journal::create` commits its record before any boundary exists and the SQLite containment row is written by a separate step — a crash in that window leaves an unsealed journal record while the barrier counts zero, so the upgrade proceeds and the new daemon inherits an obligation the barrier declared absent; (b) after any prior non-graceful daemon death under `KillMode=process`, live descendants in `executors/invocation-*` are invisible to both queries. Harm is bounded today by the same-version restriction (`version != "stillyard " + before["version"]` -> error) and by preservation of the Store/journal/backup, so this is a doctrine and evidence gap rather than an immediate corruption path — but it is the barrier the upgrade's entire safety claim rests on. Remedy: add the journal (unsealed record count, by boot_id) and a direct `executors` subtree scan (per-child `cgroup.events` `populated`, recursively) to the barrier, and record all three in barrier.json so the evidence shows independent agreement rather than one source.

SEVERITY MEDIUM — A failed upgrade leaves the coordinator stopped, and several safety checks are `assert`s or unchecked. Evidence: in scripts/upgrade-wsl-daemon.py, `subprocess.run([... "start", ...])` sits *after* the try/finally, so any exception raised between the successful `systemctl stop` and the end of the try (a rename failure, a `save()` failure on replacement.json, the `staged.exists()` unlink path, a KeyboardInterrupt) propagates with the service stopped and never restarted; with linger and no S4U task, nothing else brings it back, and the keepalive only issues `systemctl --user start` when a fresh WSL session begins. Additionally: `assert digest(staged) == args.candidate_sha256`, `assert after["store_uuid"] == before["store_uuid"]` and `assert after["daemon_generation"] != before["daemon_generation"]` are elided entirely under `python -O`/`PYTHONOPTIMIZE`, so the post-copy integrity check and the store-identity/generation-change checks are not guaranteed to run; and `start.returncode` is written into service-start.json but never tested, so a start failure is only caught indirectly by the 45s `daemon-status` poll, whose error text ("replacement did not reconnect") misattributes the cause. Remedy: wrap stop-through-swap in a try/finally that always attempts `systemctl --user start` (restoring the backup first if the swap did not commit), convert the three asserts to explicit raises, and raise on a nonzero `start.returncode` with the captured stderr. Minor related nit in the same file: it invokes bare `systemctl` (PATH-dependent) with no XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS, unlike wsl-service.py which uses `/usr/bin/systemctl` with an explicit env — run from a session without a user bus, `check=True` raises after the barrier is taken.

SEVERITY MEDIUM — Neither installer can deliver a fix to the delegation helper or the unit onto a running system, which blocks the very fix this snapshot needs. Evidence: scripts/upgrade-wsl-daemon.py replaces only `root/bin/stillyard` (it hashes, stages and renames that one path) and never touches `root/libexec/wsl-service.py` or `~/.config/systemd/user/stillyard.service`; it also never compares the installed helper against the `helper_sha256` recorded by install-wsl-daemon.py, so silent drift or hand-editing of the helper/unit is undetected at runtime. scripts/install-wsl-daemon.py refuses to run at all when either exists (`if installed.exists() or unit.exists(): parser.error("initial installation refuses an existing executable or service; use an audited upgrade")`). Failure trace: the systemd-259 delegation problem and the `--executors` hardcoding both live in the helper and the unit, so the z2 fix has no supported delivery path onto the installed y2 host — the only routes are an unaudited manual edit (invisible to all evidence files) or a destructive teardown of the Store the upgrade tool exists to preserve. Remedy: extend the upgrade tool to stage helper and unit under the same barrier (digest-pinned, `daemon-reload` after, both digests in replacement.json), and have `delegate()` verify its own file digest against a recorded anchor at startup so drift fails closed.

SEVERITY MEDIUM — Initial install never binds the installed bytes to the verified release Job; the digest check is circular. Evidence: scripts/install-wsl-daemon.py validates the Job (`state == "final"`, `outcome == "succeeded"`, label `wsl-bootstrap-build-release`) and separately checks `digest(args.candidate) != args.candidate_sha256` — but `--candidate-sha256` is operator-supplied and is compared only against the operator-supplied `--candidate`, which proves self-consistency and nothing about provenance. Contrast scripts/upgrade-wsl-daemon.py, which does bind them: it derives `target = Path(build["spec"]["environment"]["set"]["CARGO_TARGET_DIR"])/"release/stillyard"` and rejects unless `candidate == target.resolve()` and `build["spec"]["args"] == ["build","--locked","--release"]`. So the tool whose docstring promises "a validated first WSL installation" is the weaker of the two: any file at all can be installed alongside a genuine but unrelated successful gate Job, and the resulting plan.json will look fully validated. Remedy: apply the upgrade tool's CARGO_TARGET_DIR/args binding in the install path as well, and record the resolved target path in plan.json.

SEVERITY MEDIUM — Install is neither atomic nor durable, and a crash mid-install wedges both tools. Evidence: scripts/install-wsl-daemon.py uses `shutil.copyfile(args.candidate, installed)` and `shutil.copyfile(source_helper, helper)` directly to their final names (no staged temp + rename, so a truncated interrupt leaves a partial executable at the live path); it fsyncs file contents via read-only handles (`with path.open("rb") as stream: os.fsync(stream.fileno())` — permitted on Linux but fragile) and never fsyncs any containing directory (`root`, `bin`, `libexec`, `~/.config/systemd/user`), unlike the careful `publish()` in src/runner/linux/journal.rs which does `File::open(directory)?.sync_all()` after every rename/link. Failure trace: a VM shutdown or crash after `save(root/"config.json", ...)` but before the binary's directory entry is durable leaves `config.json` present and `bin/stillyard` absent or zero-length; re-running install then hits `initial installation refuses existing Store/configuration history`, while upgrade-wsl-daemon.py cannot help because its first action is `query("daemon-status")` against a binary that does not work — manual cleanup of a partially-installed Store becomes the only exit. Given no coldboot guarantee is claimed, this window is reachable. Remedy: copy to `.next-<uuid>` + fsync + rename + parent-directory fsync for binary, helper, config and unit; write an `install-in-progress` marker that install itself is permitted to reconcile, so a partial install is repairable by the tool that created it.

SEVERITY MEDIUM — Cleanup can be permanently blocked by a child cgroup, and the mitigation is only a comment. Evidence: `Boundary::kill_and_seal` in src/runner/linux/cgroup.rs writes `cgroup.kill`, waits on the (correctly recursive) `populated` flag, then ends with `std::fs::remove_dir(&self.identity.path)`; the comment states "Invocation user code sees read-only cgroups, so it cannot add child boundaries. Unexpected descendants make rmdir fail closed." Nothing in the two Linux runner files provided enforces or tests that claim — the invocation cgroup is created by the daemon under the same uid as the Invocation, and per cgroup-v2 delegation semantics a same-uid process with a writable cgroupfs view can `mkdir` inside its own cgroup. Failure trace if the read-only view is not actually in place: user code creates `executors/invocation-X/sub` -> `cgroup.kill` still kills recursively and `populated` goes to 0, so the wait loop exits -> `remove_dir` fails EBUSY on the non-empty cgroup -> `kill_and_seal` returns Err -> `Journal::cleanup` returns Err with no seal -> per doctrine no Ticket, no release, so the Lease/Grant debit is retained forever, and every retry fails identically because the child directory persists. That is a self-inflicted capacity DoS from inside a single Invocation. Uncertainty: src/runner/linux/launch.rs and the namespace/mount setup were not provided; the guarantee may well be implemented there, in which case this reduces to a missing test. Also note `contains_process` reads only the boundary's own `cgroup.procs` and is therefore non-recursive — sound at its one current call site (`Journal::ready`, before user code runs, root directly attached) but a hazard if it is ever reused for cleanup or attribution; the recursive `populated` is correctly the emptiness proof. Remedy: depth-first rmdir of any surviving descendants before removing the boundary; assert the read-only cgroupfs view at attach time; add a hostile-Invocation test that mkdirs a child cgroup and asserts the seal still completes.

SEVERITY MEDIUM-LOW — Reconnect handling amplifies any transport outage. Evidence: the error arm of the loop in src/daemon/attached.rs ends in a fixed `std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1))` with no exponential backoff, jitter, cap, or escalation after N consecutive failures; each retry calls `Driver::connect` -> `Bridge::spawn`, which re-reads and SHA-256s the *entire* Windows image on every attempt (the `loop { image.read(&mut buffer) }` block, bounded only at 512 MiB) across the DrvFs/9p boundary. Also, `exchange()` sets `self.broken = true` before the frame exchange and clears it only after correlation succeeds, so any single `DeadlineElapsed` (deadline clamped to 30s) discards the whole bridge and forces a full respawn plus rehash — correct fail-closed reasoning about stream position, but expensive. Failure trace: a stale interop alias or a Windows-side outage produces sustained 1 Hz respawn attempts, each hashing the Windows binary over the filesystem bridge, for as long as the outage lasts (indefinitely, since with linger the daemon persists); the `reported`-string dedup in the same loop suppresses repeats only while the detail text is byte-identical, so any varying errno/detail floods journald at the same cadence. Remedy: exponential backoff with cap and jitter; cache the verified image digest keyed on (dev, ino, size, mtime) and re-verify on change rather than on every attempt; distinguish and report stale-alias separately (see the interop-validation finding); add a consecutive-failure threshold that surfaces as a `daemon-status` blocker. Minor, same file: the success path does `store.lock().ok().and_then(...).unwrap_or(1s)`, silently degrading a poisoned store mutex to default polling instead of treating it as terminal.

SEVERITY MEDIUM-LOW — Keepalive leaks its alias on start failure, and its recorded lifetime story no longer matches reality. Evidence in scripts/wsl-service.py `keepalive()`: (1) `subprocess.run(["/usr/bin/systemctl", "--user", "start", "--no-block", "stillyard.service"], check=True, timeout=15)` executes *before* the `try:` whose `finally` unlinks the alias, so a CalledProcessError/TimeoutExpired there exits with a traceback and leaves `root/interop.sock` behind, pointing at a socket that dies with the session — manufacturing exactly the stale-alias state that `Bridge::spawn` does not validate; (2) `--no-block` plus `check=True` verifies only that systemctl accepted the job, never that the service reached running or that the daemon paired, so the component claiming lifetime authority has no readiness feedback; (3) `os.environ["WSL_INTEROP"]` raises a bare KeyError rather than the module's clear RuntimeError style; (4) the published record (`pid`, `boot_id`, `interop_alias`, `interop_server`) goes only to stdout — under the actual deployment (no S4U task, a detached ordinary per-user wsl.exe) that console is not captured, so the one piece of evidence that would let the daemon validate alias freshness against the current boot_id is discarded; (5) the module docstring still asserts "The Windows scheduled task runs keepalive in a foreground wsl.exe session", and install-wsl-daemon.py's docstring says "Windows keepalive registration follow[s] the saved setup receipt", yet no evidence file records which mechanism is actually in force — a reviewer reading plan.json/staged.json cannot distinguish a registered S4U task from the degraded detached fallback that exists after the access-denied/UAC-cancelled attempt. Remedy: write the receipt durably to `root/keepalive.json` (atomic replace, including boot_id and pid start_ticks) and have `Bridge::spawn` require a match; move the systemctl start inside the try/finally; raise a clear error when WSL_INTEROP is unset; record the actual keepalive mechanism and its privilege outcome in the install evidence and in `daemon-status`.
